title: LFN IPCA Report - Appendices
text:
Overview
This document describes the methods used to analyse caribou movement data. It is divided into four sections:

Summarizing data. Description of caribou movement datasets that were acquired from the Yukon and BC governments.
Defining seasons. A priori seasonal and migration date ranges and methods used to define date ranges for individual caribou.
Estimating ranges. Methods used to estimate annual and seasonal ranges.
Identifying corridors. Methods used to identify and map seasonal migration corridors.

title: Defining segments
text:
Prior to conducting any analyses, we classified GPS locations based on seasons and migration periods. For northern mountain caribou, behaviour and movement is generally divided into 4-5 seasons: calving, summer (post-calving), fall rut, and winter (early and late).

Seasonal ranges
For all home range analyses (annual and seasonal), we used seasons that were defined by the Yukon Government (Table 1).



Table 1. Seasons and date ranges for northern mountain caribou.


Season
Date range




Early winter
Nov 21 - Jan 31


Late winter
Feb 01 - May 14


Calving
May 15 - Jun 15


Summer
Jun 16 - Sep 14


Fall rut
Sep 15 - Oct 20







Seasonal migrations
Although the Yukon Government also provides definitions fpr spring and fall migration periods, we decided, due to the large variation in movement patterns, to identify seasonal migration periods for each individual for each year. To do this we used Net Squared Displacement (NSD) analysis combined with visual inspection of the spatial distribution of GPS locations using the BEACONs Movement Mapper app to identify spring and fall migration start and end dates for each individual in each year. Migration periods were defined as follows:

Spring migration: Movement from winter range to summer range (generally northeast direction), beginning when individuals depart the winter range and ending upon arrival at summer range
Fall migration: Movement from summer range to winter range (generally southwest direction), beginning when individuals depart the summer range and ending upon arrival at winter range


Workflow
We used the Movement Mapper app to identify start and end dates for spring and fall migration periods for each individual in each year.

For each individual/year:

Visualize movement tracks on map with seasonal color coding
Review NSD vs. day-of-year plots
Identify migration periods using these criteria:

Spring migration start: First sustained increase in NSD (e.g., >20% increase maintained for >7 days)
Spring migration end: NSD plateau or reversal indicating arrival at summer range
Fall migration start: First sustained decrease in NSD from summer range
Fall migration end: NSD plateau indicating establishment on winter range

Adjust date sliders to refine start/end dates based on visual assessment
If clear spring and fall migrations exist: Record start/end dates for both periods
If no evidence of migration assign NA to migration dates
Document ambiguous cases with comments in the notes field


Notes:
The first challenge in mapping a migration is figuring out when an animal is actually migrating versus when it is simply living in its seasonal home range. An individual caribou might wander for several kilometres in its summer territory, but that isn’t the same as its focused, directional journey between seasons. To solve this, we can use analytical tool called Net Squared Displacement (NSD). In simple terms, NSD measures the straight-line distance an animal is from a fixed starting point, which is typically set near the beginning of the biological year (e.g., January 1) within the animal’s winter range, and then squares that value. When plotted on a graph over a full year, the NSD curve for a migrating animal reveals a distinct, three-phase pattern:

In the starting range: When an individual is settled in its winter or summer range, it stays relatively close to the starting point. The NSD value fluctuates a little but remains low, creating a relatively flat line on the graph.
During migration: As the individual begins its journey to its summer or winter range, it moves steadily away from the starting point. This causes the NSD value to increase sharply and consistently, creating a steep upward slope on the graph.
In the target range: Once the individual arrives and settles in its summer or winter range, it is far from the starting point, so the NSD value is high. However, because it is no longer moving in a single direction, the value stabilizes and flattens out again at this new, higher level.

The “clear breakpoints” on the graph – where the line begins to rise and where it flattens out – allow us to identify the exact start and end dates of the spring and fall migrations. All the locations recorded between these dates are then grouped together, forming a single “migration sequence” for that animal in that year.

title: Estimating ranges
text:
Overview
Estimating the boundaries of seasonal and annual caribou ranges is an important step in effective wildlife conservation and management. Defining these spatial limits allows managers to identify core habitat areas, including calving grounds and winter foraging areas. This information is fundamental for land use planning, as it ensures that development and human activities are regulated to minimize disturbance and avoid habitat loss and fragmentation within these key areas. Ultimately, understanding and mapping caribou ranges provides the necessary baseline data to implement targeted conservation measures, monitor population health in relation to their environment, and support sustainable resource management for the long-term persistence of the herds.
We estimated annual and seasonal ranges using locations collected from many caribou over multiple years. To understand how herds use the landscape across the year, we grouped these locations into biologically meaningful seasons: annual, early winter, late winter, summer, and the fall rut. For each season, we used a statistical mapping approach called a kernel density estimator (KDE), implemented in R using the amt package. This method creates smooth contours around clusters of points, showing where caribou spend most of their time. The outer contour (the 95% isopleth) represents the broader seasonal range, while the inner contour (the 50% isopleth) highlights the core areas most heavily used.
This approach provides a consistent way to compare how different herds use space and how their ranges shift across seasons. Because it summarizes many individual movement paths into a single population‑level map, it helps identify key habitats and areas that may require conservation attention. The graphic below illustrates the concept, showing points, the estimated 95% range boundary, and the 50% core area for an example herd.
Individual-level range estimation
For each individual/year/season, use the Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) method to estimate probability density functions of animal locations, resulting in utilization distributions.
Parameters: Select appropriate smoothing parameters (e.g., h-value) using methods like Likelihood Cross-Validation (LCV) or reference bandwidth.
Output: Generate 95% and 50% (or other relevant contours) utilization distributions (UDs) for annual and seasonal ranges for each individual for each year. The former (95%) represents the overall annual or seasonal range while the latter (50% isopleths) represents core or high use areas.
Population-level range estimation
There are two broad approaches that could be used to estimate population-level annual and seasonal ranges:

Method 1 - Union of individual ranges: Combine individual ranges (e.g., 95% KDEs) to visualize the total area used by the population annually and seasonally.
Method 2 - Population-level estimates: Pool all individual locations for a given period and estimate a single population-level range that represents the overall utilization distribution.

We used the second method to estimate population-level ranges and the resulting maps are available in the main section of the report (Section 9).
Interactive dashboard
In addition, to the maps in the report, we developed an interactive dashboard to assist in visualizing 1) individual- and population-level annual and seasonal range estimates and 2) variation in range estimates between individuals, years, and seasons.

Step 2. Make tracks
Tracks are the basic building blocks of movement analysis in the amt package. So, we first use the make_track function for convert our data.frame into tracks. Note that we have to specify the crs of the data which, in this case, is lat-long or “EPSG:4326”. We can then project our coordinates to the Yukon Albers projection using the transform_coords function.











Step 3. Estimate ranges
Geometric estimators: MCP
Geometric estimators such as minimum convex polygons(MCP) only rely on the observed locations and can only estimate the occurrence distribution (i.e., where the animal was during the study period). MCPs can be constructed with multiple levels using the function hr_mcp() from the amt package.

MCPs can be viewed as isopleths.









Probabilistic estimators (KDE)
Probabilistic estimators (e.g., KDEs) are based on an underlying model for the utilization distribution (UD). They can estimate the occurrence distribution or the range distribution (where the animal could be found at any future time if its movement process remains the same) depending on the underlying model. Can be represented as a hull by outlining a cumulative probability of use. Fitting a KDE to telemetry data is the same problem as with MCPs, but in 2 dimensions. Choosing a bandwidth is important to the final result, and there are multiple possible methods for doing so. Here, we will focus on the reference bandwidth, whic is the default.

title: Identifying corridors
text:
Overview
Overview of the importance of identifying and mapping seasonal movement corridors for caribou.


Walkthrough
In this section we describe the steps used to estimate individual home ranges using the KDE approach and compare it to another commonly used method, the minimum convex hull (MCP). We illustrate the approach for one individual caribou.

Step 1. Identify migration periods
This step is described in “Seasonal migrations” in the “Defining segments” section.


Step 2. Map individual paths
Simply connecting the dots of a migration sequence with a straight line gives a rough idea of the route, but it’s an oversimplification. It doesn’t reveal the true width of the path or, more importantly, the specific areas where an animal stopped-over to rest and feed. To build a more realistic map, we used a statistical method called the Brownian Bridge Movement Model (BBMM). This model is incorporates a key parameter called the Brownian motion variance (BMV), which is a statistical estimate of an individual’s mobility, making the resulting map more realistic. The output of this model is a utilization distribution (UD), which is essentially a “heat map” or “probability surface.” Instead of just showing a line, the UD shows the likelihood of an individual having been in any given location along its route. The “hotter” the color, the more time the individual likely spent there.
Using a BBMM to create a utilization distribution has two major benefits:

Estimates path width: The model calculates the probable width of the movement path around the straight lines connecting the points. This transforms a simple line into a more realistic two-dimensional corridor, showing the full area the individual may have used.
Identifies stopover sites: The “hottest” parts of the heat map are incredibly valuable. They reveal stopover sites - critical areas where animals spend extended time foraging and resting during their long journey. These sites are as important to the success of a migration as the path itself.






Figure 1. Brownian bridge movement model (95% contour) for one caribou in 2021.






Step 3. Average individual paths
To protect a migration, we need to see the main corridor used by the entire population, not just the path of one individual. This can be achieved this by combining all the individual maps into a single, comprehensive view of the herd’s movement. This involves a three step process:

Average individual migrations: First, for each individual, we took all of its yearly migration UDs (the heat maps) and average them together. This creates a single map representing the typical migration path for that specific animal over time.
Define individual footprints: For each animal’s averaged map, we defined its “footprint” as the area that contains 99% of its probable locations. This captures the vast majority of where that individual traveled.
Stack the footprints: All of these individual footprints are then layered, or “stacked” on top of one another. The result is a map where every pixel on the grid has a value corresponding to how many different individuals passed through it.






Figure 2. Movement paths based on BBMM models for all caribou in all years.






Step 4. Classify corridors
Finally, we can classify the resultant stacked map to visualize how 1) intensely different parts of the corridor are used by the herd and 2) where the key stopovers areas are located. This allows us to distinguish between occasional and essential parts of the corridor.
Output 1: Corridor use intensity
The levels of corridor use are typically defined as follows:








Use Level
Definition
Importance




Low Use
Areas used by at least one individual.
Shows the maximum extent of the entire migration footprint.


Medium Use
Areas used by 10-20% of the individuals.
Represents regularly used routes.


High Use
Areas used by >20% of individuals.
Pinpoints the most critical, core pathways essential for the herd’s survival.



 Output 2: High use areas
High use areas or stopovers are areas where animals spend extended time foraging and resting during migration. They are defined as the top 10% of use values from the propulation-level probability map. Protecting these high-use areas is as important as protecting the connectivity between them.





Figure 3. High use areas within movement paths.
